cultivar: Zhenghe Da Bai Cha (政和大白茶)
processing: Single buds withered and dried with no firing or rolling. The method is the same as other silver needle; the difference from Fuding comes from the plant and the place.
harvest_season: Early spring, when the buds are still closed; the first flush buds are the ones wanted, as with all silver needle.
appearance_dry: Plump single buds covered in silvery down.
appearance_wet: Fleshy whole buds, soft and pale green-yellow.
taste_profile: Fuller and rounder than its Fuding cousin, with a clear fragrance, hay sweetness and a smooth, gently vegetal finish.

brewing.notes: Buds give up flavour slowly. Use cooler water than for leafy white teas and let the steeps run longer; rushing gives a thin cup.

vintage_note: Usually sold as the current year's spring harvest, with the year stated. Like other silver needle it can also be kept and sold with age, though the buds change more slowly and cost more than leafier grades. Ask for the year and the cultivar, since Zhenghe buds and Fuding buds look alike to a casual eye.
description:
Silver needle splits into two old lines: the northern one from Fuding and the southern one from Zhenghe. This is the southern line, made from single buds of the local Zhenghe Da Bai Cha plant in the hills at the eastern foot of the Wuyi range.

The making is as spare as white tea gets: pick the buds, wither them, dry them. No firing and no rolling. So the character comes from the bud itself, and Zhenghe's buds are generally described as giving a thicker, more rounded cup than Fuding's, with Fuding's reading lighter and more downy.

In the cup, expect clean fragrance and sweet hay rather than strong flower, and a body that is noticeable for such a pale liquor. Most disappointing cups come from short steeps in a hurry. Give the buds time, and do not use boiling water if you want the sweetness up front.

It is sold under the plain name Bai Hao Yin Zhen far more often than with Zhenghe on the label, so the origin is the first thing to ask about. Comparing it side by side with a Fuding needle from the same year is the fastest way to learn what the two lines are.
history:
Zhenghe was a tea producing area by the late Tang and early Song, and it supplied the Beiyuan tribute tea. Local tradition and a 2024 China News Service article say that in 1115 Emperor Huizong was so pleased with a white tea tribute from Guanli county that he gave it the name of his reign era, Zhenghe. Treat this as a county origin story: the name Bai Hao Yin Zhen applied to a Song tribute tea is not the same as evidence of today's method.

The modern north and south division rests on cultivars, with Fuding Da Bai Hao in the north and Zhenghe Da Bai Cha in the south. Zhenghe today is counted among the core white tea counties of China.
